title: Bits on the wire
summary: What voltage, photons, and radio actually carry your packet, and why the speed of light bounds everything above.
crux: What voltage, photons, and radio actually carry your packet, and why the speed of light bounds everything above.
keytakeaway: Every byte of Internet traffic travels as voltage on copper, light pulses through glass fibre, or modulated radio waves through air. The medium has a bandwidth (bits per second, determined by Shannon's theorem) and a propagation delay (length divided by signal speed, ~200,000 km/s in fibre). Higher protocols layer on top but cannot beat these physics — a New-York-to-Sydney request will always take at least ~200 ms round-trip. Practical engineering means knowing the floor numbers, recognising bandwidth-bound vs latency-bound problems, and applying the right fix: more parallelism / wider links / compression for bandwidth, or CDN edges / cache hits / round-trip elimination for latency.
misconceptions: Heads-up: bandwidth is not latency :: You cannot solve latency by buying bandwidth. A 10 Gb/s link doesn't move one byte faster than 100 Mb/s — bytes travel at light speed. More bandwidth increases throughput, not speed. Pre-position data (CDN) or eliminate round-trips (HTTP/2 push, QUIC 0-RTT, TLS resumption).

You never learn to shrink packets, retransmit at 1500 bytes forever, hitting ~1 second timeouts. TCP MSS clamping and assuming 1280-byte MTU mitigate this in practice.

title: The TCP handshake

keytakeaway: TCP's three-way handshake exchanges and acknowledges starting sequence numbers in both directions before any byte of application data flows, costing one full RTT per connection. Modern Linux protects the handshake with SYN cookies under flood, replaces the loss-based congestion control of Reno with CUBIC or BBR for lossy long-RTT paths, and uses RACK-TLP to detect loss faster than the classic RTO timer. Above the protocol layer the operational concerns are TIME-WAIT exhaustion (fix with connection pools + tcp_tw_reuse), Nagle/delayed-ACK stalls (fix with TCP_NODELAY), and kernel-tunable hygiene for any service handling thousands of handshakes per second.
misconceptions: Heads-up: SYN floods aren't dead :: SYN cookies mitigate classic SYN floods but ignore TCP options like timestamps. Modern attacks layer SYN floods with TLS ClientHellos, starving handshake CPU. Defence is layered: rate limits, connection priming, and abuse-pattern detection.

title: TLS 1.3: keys and confidentiality in one RTT
summary: How ClientHello key shares plus a certificate verifier collapse the old TLS 1.2 two-RTT handshake into one — and what 0-RTT actually buys you.
crux: How key shares and ECDHE collapse TLS 1.2's two-RTT handshake into one, and what 0-RTT buys you.
keytakeaway: TLS 1.3 collapses the handshake to one RTT by sending the client's ECDHE key share inside ClientHello, mandates ephemeral key exchange so every session has Perfect Forward Secrecy, and supports 0-RTT resumption — but 0-RTT must be restricted to idempotent methods or replay attacks turn the optimisation into a duplicate-write disaster. Above that protocol layer sits the post-2024 operational frontier: hybrid post-quantum key shares, Encrypted ClientHello, kernel-TLS offload, and CRLite-style revocation that finally replaces soft-fail OCSP.
misconceptions: Heads-up: 0-RTT replay :: 0-RTT data is not protected against replay attacks. An attacker on the wire can capture a 0-RTT ClientHello and resend it to the server. title: QUIC internals
summary: How QUIC merges UDP, transport logic, and TLS into a fast, multiplexed protocol that runs entirely in user space and survives network path changes.
crux: How QUIC merges UDP, transport logic, and TLS into a fast protocol that multiplexes streams and survives network migration.
keytakeaway: QUIC fuses UDP, TLS 1.3, and transport multiplexing into a user-space protocol that completes its handshake in 1 RTT (vs TCP+TLS 2–3 RTT), eliminates head-of-line blocking via independent streams (575× latency improvement on lossy paths), and survives network migration via connection IDs. The trade-off is CPU cost (15–30% higher per byte than kernel TCP, up to ~45% goodput loss on fast links). Deployment is phased: mobile clients benefit from QUIC's latency and HoL elimination; desktop and high-throughput paths remain TCP. UDP blocking in ~3–5% of networks requires mandatory fallback to HTTP/2. Operationally, QUIC encryption breaks traditional packet inspection, demanding application-level observability and tracing infrastructure. The protocol is now 5 years old (RFC 9000, 2021) with ~21% web-traffic adoption, ~35–40% of major sites advertising support, and steady growth as client implementations mature and hardware offload reduces CPU cost.
misconceptions: Heads-up: QUIC is fragile to UDP blocking :: 3–5% of networks block UDP outright. When silently dropped, QUIC times out and falls back to HTTP/2, adding latency. Browsers race QUIC and TCP in parallel, so whichever succeeds first wins. Fallback to HTTP/2 must be seamless.

title: Putting it together: one HTTPS request, end to end

Security hardening (mTLS for service mesh, WAF for edge, rate limiting for DDoS) must not be retrofitted; design it in from layer 1. The operational frontier is distributed tracing with W3C Trace Context, USE/RED method-based instrumentation, circuit breakers for cascade isolation, and error-budget-driven release cadence — all of which give you the vocabulary to debug, design, and ship performant, resilient network-bound systems.

title: OAuth 2.1 and OIDC: delegated authorization that does not leak
summary: PKCE-required auth code flow, refresh token rotation, ID tokens, DPoP and mTLS-bound tokens, and the JWKS validation pitfalls that actually leak data.
crux: How to let one app act on a user's behalf in another app without ever seeing the password — and without leaking the access.
keytakeaway: OAuth 2.1 = PKCE everywhere, exact redirect match, refresh rotation, no implicit. OIDC adds signed id_tokens for identity. DPoP or mTLS for sender-constrained tokens against theft.
